name: Microsoft COCO (Common Objects in Context)
description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation in natural scenes. The dataset contains photos of 91 object types that would be easily recognizable by a 4 year old, with objects labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. Images depict complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick, "Microsoft COCO: Common objects in context," in ECCV, 2014.
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using a novel pipeline that queries for pairs of objects in conjunction with scene-based queries to gather non-iconic images containing contextual relationships. The dataset employed searches for pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') and scene/object category pairs rather than single object categories to find natural images containing multiple objects in their natural context. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. In rare cases where enough images could not be found, single category searches were performed with explicit filtering to remove iconic images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were sourced from Flickr, a photo-sharing platform containing photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A filtering stage was applied to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate images. Workers were shown grids of 128 candidate images and asked to remove iconic images (images with single large objects in canonical perspectives centered in the image) and invalid images. Instructions included examples of iconic and non-iconic images to guide workers.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary stages: (1) Category labeling: 8 workers per image used a hierarchical approach to label object categories present, dragging category icons onto one instance of each category. A category was considered present if any worker indicated it. (2) Instance spotting: 8 workers per image placed crosses on top of each instance of categories found in the previous stage, labeling at most 10 instances per category per image. Workers were primed with the location of one instance from the previous stage and could use a magnifying glass to find small instances. (3) Instance segmentation: Workers segmented each object instance using a modified version of the OpenSurfaces interface. All workers completed a training task for each object category requiring them to match ground truth segmentations before being allowed to segment instances. Each instance was segmented by a single worker. For images with more than 10-15 instances of a category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single (possibly multi-part) segment. A verification stage was added where 3-5 workers judged each segmentation; segmentations receiving fewer than 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded and re-queued.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker quality was analyzed by comparing AMT workers to expert workers (co-authors). The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any individual expert worker on category labeling. For category labeling, ground truth was computed using majority vote of experts. A leave-one-out evaluation showed most workers had high precision. Workers who completed the most jobs also had the highest precision; all jobs from workers below a quality threshold were rejected. The training task for segmentation filtered out approximately 1 in 3 workers, vastly improving segmentation quality.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Category labeling: 8 workers per image. Instance spotting: 8 workers per image. Instance segmentation: 1 worker per instance. Segmentation verification: 3-5 workers per segmentation.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The MS COCO dataset is split into two roughly equal parts. The first half was released in 2014, containing 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The second half was planned for release in 2015, with the cumulative release containing a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. The 2014 release was limited to a subset of 80 categories, with potential addition of segmentations for some of the remaining 11 categories in the cumulative 2015 release.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently only labels 'things' (objects for which individual instances may be easily labeled) and not 'stuff' categories (materials and objects with no clear boundaries like sky, street, grass). The dataset is limited to entry-level categories rather than fine-grained categories or object-part categories. Some categories were removed because obtaining a large number of instances (greater than 5,000) was difficult. The 2014 release excluded 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (due to confusion with bowl and dining table), and blender, hair brush (too few instances).
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for object detection and segmentation tasks. It is intended to advance the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing object recognition in the context of scene understanding. The dataset can be used for training and evaluating algorithms for: detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization of objects. Baseline performance analysis was provided for bounding box and segmentation detection using a Deformable Parts Model. The dataset enables learning detailed object models capable of precise 2D localization and learning contextual information due to the high number of object instances per image.
